utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution assisted by Denise Gustin case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Milan Trbojevic and my associate Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you too. Before we proceed, Ms. Sutherland, I would like to know which municipality to expect immediately after Prijedor. If you have the order --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi. We can provide Your Honour and the Defence with a list of the order of the witnesses very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So the next witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next witness has protective measures, BT33. Her evidence will be heard in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.134, just let me check to make sure. Yes. So usher, please prepare the courtroom for closed session. Please, let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour before we begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Rupert Read, law clerk from the Office of the Prosecutor has joined us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome and good morning to you. One thing, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Trbojevic, it occurred to me and my attention has actually been drawn also to the fact that referring to the previous witness, the transcript of her testimony in Stakic shows that at a certain point in time, what was an open session and subsequently a private session, and then open session, et cetera, turned out to be a closed session, which makes it important to take some precautionary action over here and I was going to suggest to you -- since it's not feasible to divide the transcript into different parts, parts which are open, parts which are private, parts which are closed, I was going to suggest to the Defence and the Prosecution to agree that Exhibit P1544 will be accepted, admitted, under seal. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's it. Let me -- the next witness, 7.54, I understand has not asked for any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Nasic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. This is the first time you are giving evidence and therefore I need to explain to you very short -- and very briefly what is important for you to know. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath. That in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that the usher is going to hand to you after which I would invite you to stand up and read that declaration aloud and that would be your solemn undertaking with us that in the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. You will be conducting the examination-in-chief, Ms. Sutherland will be now examining you in chief, putting a series of questions to you, which you are required to answer. After that, you will be cross-examined by the Defence team. Now, your duty is not to make any distinction between the Prosecution and the Defence. You're duty is to answer each and every question, irrespective of who is putting the question to you, as truthfully and as completely as you can. Incidentally, what you see in this courtroom, I need to explain very briefly. Right in front of you, in the front row, is the Registrar's staff. They will be following the proceedings as they go along. And I am the Presiding Judge, my name is Carmen Agius, I come from Malta and I'm flanked at my right by Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and on the left by Judge Taya from Japan. The team for the Prosecution is to your right. You need only be concerned with Ms. Sutherland, who will be cross-examining you. It's not that the others are not important but for the time being, that's -- and then you will be cross-examined, I presume by Mr. Trbojevic who is co-counsel for the accused Mr. Brdjanin. Yes you may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Elvedin Nasic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on the 1st of July, 1971 in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In 1971, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your nickname is Vedo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ethnicity is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, you provided a statement to the CSB in Banja Luka about events which occurred in the Prijedor municipality in 1992, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January, 1995, you were interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In March, 2000, you were again interviewed by an investigator and a lawyer from the Office of the Prosecutor where you made some changes to your 1995 statement and provided some additional information?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January, 2002, you were visited by members of the Tribunal when they took a declaration from you and you made some additional changes to the statements taken in 1995 and 2000?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January and February, 2002, you had a brief conversation with an investigator in respect of another case. Do you recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic, you spoke some limited English. However, I would ask that you wait for the translation into your native language before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to deal with a sensitive matter for one moment and I would ask that we go into closed session to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Madam Registrar, let's go into closed session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are -- I notice that we are in private session. I said closed session. You said closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So keep it in private session, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Ms. Sutherland. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic in May, 1992, you were residing in the village of Hambarine in the municipality of Prijedor with your parents, your three brothers and your two sisters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up until that time, you had lived in Hambarine all your life?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1990 and 1991, you completed your compulsory JNA military training and you specialised in firing ammunition from tanks?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a gunner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May, 1992, you were 21 years old and worked as a mechanic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I was 21 but I had already completed my schooling. However, I was not employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the TO in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover of power by the Serbs in Prijedor, on the 30th of April, 1992, did your village set up night patrols?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in those patrols?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I did occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to events that occurred in May, 1992. According to your recollection, on or about the 21st of May, 1992, an incident occurred at the Muslim checkpoint in Hambarine? After that incident, was an ultimatum given to hand over weapons and the Muslim men who were at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the ultimatum given?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It was aired on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was stated, if the ultimatum wasn't met?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact details of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred the following day in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: The following day, since the weapons were not surrendered, nor did the people who were at the checkpoint surrendered, then sometime around 12.00 or around that time, the general attack on Hambarine started. Some occasional shells landed on neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the shelling continuous or intermittent?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Initially, it was continuous and then afterwards, it was intermittent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what direction the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Since I was a gunner, one tank was positioned in the area of Tukovi and the artillery, the mortars were firing from Miljakovci. I'm not sure whether that was the exact area but around there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people that lived in the village of Miljakovci, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There were Muslims and -- but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did the shelling last?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I can't be -- I'm not going to be very specific about that but probably for several hours, three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, we made some kind of a zone of defence for the village. Just in case. In order to protect the population, and in order to enable the inhabitants to flee into the neighbouring woods in case of an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I was with my neighbours on the positions. I was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay on the position for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I think two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see from that position?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We didn't see much. However, we could feel, we could see the shells flying by and landing all over the village. The mosque was targeted quite a lot. It was targeted and we could see it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the village, where were -- where was the position where you were at?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: At the entry point into the village, looking from Prijedor, we were to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the mosque was targeted quite a lot. Were any -- could you see any damage to any of the houses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Some were damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, did tanks and soldiers enter the village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. After we had withdrawn, the civilians withdrew, then we withdrew, and then they entered. With one or two tanks, I'm not sure, because I was not present because we had already left the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers before you left the village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We went into the neighbouring wood, which was called Kurevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Kurevo forest?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We spent there three days and then I went to my aunt's because she was in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with your parents and your brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: During the first three nights, yes. And later on, they went to Donja Ljubija where there was a refugee centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said you went to your aunt's house. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That was in the local commune of Donja Ljubija. It was close to the Kurevo woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend at your aunt's place?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Not long. I would go there only occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you weren't at your aunt's house, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We were hiding in the woods, the same woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were hiding in the woods with you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: During the first day, we had small groups of some 10, 20, 30 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the woods for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: About a month, to month and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people that were in the woods, how many of them were armed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. After the villages were cleansed, the neighbouring villages, such as Biscani, Rakovcani, Rizvanovici, Carakovo, there were some 300 to 400 civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when these villages were cleansed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Biscani, Rakovcani, and Rizvanovici, around the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently visit or go to these villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage to the houses in the villages?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: A lot of houses had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in all three villages or one or two in particular?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In all three villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the forest, was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Since the village of Carakovo was cleansed after the first three villages, four young men were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness their killing or were you told about it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally. However, we heard from the people that were with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the woods, did you meet up with a person called Asim Mujic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, as a group, leave the forest?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We started towards the free territory, towards Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were there in your group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: About 50 to 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you -- you started towards the free territory. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened as you went towards the free territory?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: At night, I can't exactly remember the date, we set out towards the free territory. There were 50 to 60 in our group. As we passed through other forests, which were privately owned, we were joined by other groups so that in the end, there were about 200 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what direction were you heading?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That night, we walked towards the village of Kalajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that towards Bihac?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Our aim was to reach not just Bihac but any place in the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people in this group were armed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: A few. I don't know how many exactly, but some did have some personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: The next day, around 11.00, we were in the village of Kalajevo, and we were discovered there by Serb troops, and at that moment, they opened fire. We scattered in groups so that a group of about 120 went on. That same day, sometime in late afternoon, at dusk, we entered or rather we were passing -- passing and unaware where we were going, we entered the village of Miska Glava, and when we got there, that is we were in the woods nearby, and two guys went to the first house to find out where exactly we had fetched up. However, when they reached that house, a man came out and we could hear a shot. Meanwhile, troops were coming from behind our backs so that we were surrounded, and then they took us to a meadow where we were lined up in four columns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were there that surrounded the group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: About 20, maybe more. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed and were they carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Some of them were in olive-green grey uniforms and others were in camouflage uniforms. There were some individuals wearing those. And they were well armed. They had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were put into this column, what were you made to do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: We were lined up in foursomes and then we headed off in some direction, I don't know which, and then again we stopped in a place, in a valley, and we waited for some transportation, because after that, we were put in a van and taken further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in this valley, did anyone try to escape?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, before that, as the column started on its way, a man whose last name is Crljenkovic, I believe, his first name is Mustafa, he tried to escape but failed. He was killed. He was hit in the head. And he was killed from -- by a bullet from a rifle called PAP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were two men selected from your group who then buried this Mustafa Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Crljenkovic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke a moment ago about being put in a van and being taken further on. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: There was one van. They took us to the community centre in Miska Glava, took us to a place, I think it was a coffee bar or a tavern, something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were put into the -- taken to the coffee bar/tavern?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there, there were lots of troops, I don't know how many, but lots of them, and they were even bringing their wives and children to look, to see us, to observe us. That night, nothing special happened. Some who went out to relieve themselves were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your names taken?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if it was that night or perhaps the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any event, they were?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right. They took down the names. A man called Zoran, I believe his last name is Petrovic but I'm not really 100 per cent sure, I know he used to work in the veterinary pharmacy before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The veterinary pharmacy, was it in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miska Glava, approximately how far away is that from Hambarine, do you know? And in which direction?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres in the Hambarine-Ljubija direction, there are some other villages, too. Surkovac. That direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were staying at Miska Glava, while you were detained in Miska Glava, was anyone mistreated, apart from the people that you mentioned that received a beating when they went out to relieve themselves?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, as they already had the list, they called out names and because in this community centre, there were also some offices, I suppose that was the neighbourhood community, the local community office, centre. And then they called people out, took them there to interrogate them, and beat them along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you called out for questioning?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: As I entered that room, and it was quite small, perhaps 3 by 3, 3 by 4 metres, I'm not sure, but in any event, we had to keep our hands behind our neck, and had to look down at the chest, so that I can't really give you the precise size of the room. As I entered it, two or three soldiers who were standing in there right at the entrance would start dealing blows. With whatever they could lay their hands on, with rifle butts, with their fists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Miska Glava?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Two, three, or four days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone called out and taken away, never to be seen again?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Ten guys from the village of Rizvanovici were called out and they were told to come out, but they didn't, and then a soldier came and then he pointed at those ten guys to come out. And most of them came from that village, from Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ismet Hamulic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of them. He was my school fellow. He came from Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other men that were called out and taken away?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after four or five days?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: They took us in a bus towards Gornja Ljubija. That is where the football stadium was, and that is where they beat us up and some were killed even, including a relative of mine, Irfan Nasic my first cousin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to that in a little more detail in a moment. When you were first put on the bus in Miska Glava, did the bus stop anywhere before it reached the football stadium in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It stopped -- now, what shall I explain it? In Gornja Ljubija, something like the centre of Gornja Ljubija or not far from it, and there was the entrance into the mine, that is where the mine gate was. And when we stopped there, as we stopped there, a policeman called Simo came on. He was an active policeman in the former police, or whatever it was called, and he merely cast a look at us. I remember him well. He just looked at us and then got off, and after him, uniformed soldiers came on. They were wearing overalls, dark blue and black camouflage, disrupted pattern coverall uniforms, and later on, I heard there was some kind of an intervention platoon, and in the bus, they also beat with whatever -- with their boots, anything, but mostly kicking people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these intervention platoon soldiers -- people armed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. They didn't have -- when they entered the bus, they didn't have any rifles with them, but I assume they had pistols. That was when they entered the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the bus continued towards the Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: The football stadium was at the entrance into Gornja Ljubija, so the bus entered Gornja Ljubija, then made a turn and went back to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1127, the map of Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, using the pointer, can you point to where the Ljubija football stadium is on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the audio-visual director please zoom into Ljubija? And if the map could be moved slightly up? Further? Further? And across to the right a little and further up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point now to where the Ljubija football stadium is located?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is just above the word "Ljubija" and the red line that goes across the map?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right. If you are looking to -- if you are -- if you face Donja Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point now to where the iron ore mine is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: [indicates] Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're pointing now, you're circling the place where it says, "Rudnik" -- where it says, "Rudnik Zeljezne;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: "Ljubija Zeljezne Rude."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is to the south-west of the town of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the place called Rudnik Ljubija, which is to the south -- just south-west of the town of Ljubija, a short distance from it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there another name for that mine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point on the map to where the Kipe mine is?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That is a locality called Kipe. I don't think it is -- Kipe we called Rudnik, that is the mine, this whole area. Kipe I guess, is the name of a -- just of a locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what direction is that mine, is that locality?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really see it here. I think it is somewhere here to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have another map here with Miska Glava highlighted, because unfortunately, it is just off this map. So if we could have this map marked as P1546? And if that could be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, that map, this map is being admitted as Exhibit P1546. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is that -- where it's marked Miska Glava, is that the place where you were taken when you were first surrounded by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the map. Mr. Nasic, what happened when you arrived at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: At the entrance into the stadium or rather as we got off the bus, there were quite a number of civilians there who were already there when the buses came to the mine for the first time, and as we got off the bus, one of those civilians managed to hit us, and we entered -- we were entering the part of the stadium facing the stands. It was an area of some five, perhaps six metres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides these number of civilians you said who hit you as you got off the bus, besides these people and the people that you said were part of the intervention platoon, were there -- were there anyone -- was there anyone else at the stadium, any policemen, for example?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one. I didn't know him well, but we all called him by his nickname, which was Stiven. I believe he was with the police reserve force. He personally killed my relative, my cousin. There was another man there, who was a military, with a rank of a captain. That is he had the patch on his blouse, but I think it was a rank. He obtained -- he was conferred upon for war, for valour, because he didn't have it on his epaulettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you beaten with?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you beaten with, as you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Anything, you name it, metal rods, baseball bats, rifle butts, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Stiven personally killed your cousin. You mentioned his name before, Irfan Nasic. Can you explain to the Court how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Since we were the first ones to enter that area, facing the stands, to the left was the retaining wall and to the right was wire, wire fence, and in front of us were the stands. Some were singled out and moved over to the wire and others were sent to the other side, to that retaining wall. And I was in the latter group. And my cousin was on the other side, next to the wire. And he was the first one in the -- in the line. And meanwhile, Stiven, with one or two guys carrying weapons, was taking one of ours, one of the guys from our group, and asking him about what kind of weapons each one of us had. And this man from our group said that my relative had a zolja, but that was not true, because I know that he didn't have any weapons at all. And Stiven approached him, since he had his back on him, and fired a pistol at him and killed him on the spot. And another man called Muharem Crljenkovic, he opened fire from an automatic rifle and with a burst of fire, he cut his head off. I saw that with my own eyes. And moreover, he would say afterwards, "Look at this. This man didn't even have any brains." I don't know, they were making jokes, I guess, but that's what they said, "Look at this one, he didn't even have any brains in." The third man was killed but I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone called Muharem Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came from Rakovcani, a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he at the stadium that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: He was the man whose head was split into two by a gun -- burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you were actually referring to Muharem Petrovac when you mentioned a man called Muharem Crljenkovic a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can't remember the first name. I don't know whether the first name was Muharem. I know that the last name was Crljenkovic. I knew him well. We used to play football together. His nickname was Duca, this man called Crljenkovic that was killed in Miska Glava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Crljenkovic was killed in Miska Glava but it was Muharem Petrovac that was killed with Irfan Nasic, your cousin, at the Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone besides Stiven?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I recognised somebody called Predrag Vasiljevic from Ljeskare. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the neighbouring village from Hambarine, across the river?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's a village on the road from Hambarine to Ljubija, the following village after ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated again that day at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat us. They hit me with a metal baton on the head. And I lost my consciousness then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you regained consciousness?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I lay on the floor, on the concrete floor. An armed soldier kicked me with his boots saying, "Get up." He cursed my mother. That was their custom. I got up and then he said, "The two of you," since there was a young man next to me, "Pick up these dead bodies and take them elsewhere." We moved them just a few metres from the place where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was Irfan Nasic, Muharem Petrovac and a third man whose name you don't recall, whom you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of these intervention platoon men? Was anyone in particular in charge, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself to us by his first and last name but I only remember the nickname Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had moved the bodies a few metres, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: After that, in columns by three, four or five, with our hands behind our necks, and legs spread apart, started moving towards the bus, which was a double bus. As we were leaving the stadium, they beat us too with baseball bats, here in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where were you pointing to? The -- for the record, you're pointing to the side of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His right-hand side of the body, below the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, they stood on both sides. As we were leaving the stadium, we would have to pass two soldiers, standing on each side. One of them was Predrag Vasiljevic. He stood on the right, to the right of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Upon entering the bus, there were numerous armed soldiers. We entered the bus, or boarded, or whatever you want to call that. They even threw in the dead bodies into the bus. Since I was at the end of the bus, they were with us. And when everything was ready, the bus started in the direction unknown to us. Immediately after the bus started, one of the soldiers asked us first whether we wanted to go to Kurevo, and then he made us sing some of their songs. "Who is saying that Serbia is little, small?" "All of the guards are that of General Draza." The bus travelled for some 20 minutes. I'm not quite sure but approximately that long. And then it stopped. I don't know how many armed people there were on the bus. They got off, whereas one with PAP rifle stood by the driver's seat, by the door there. And he told us that we should go out in groups of three. Upon leaving the bus, some 10 to 15 seconds, a half minute later, one could hear gunfire. After the gunfire, he would call out the names of others, until our turn came. The names of me and two other young men who came out with me were called out. Upon leaving the bus, and I was the third in my group, the first two that got off lay down by the bus immediately. I was the third to get off, and I expected to hear the shots. However, something else was going on, because when I met the two young men later, who were with me, that evening, while we were descending, they broke the window and jumped off the bus so that they drew their attention to them and the soldiers that were armed started chasing them because four or five of them jumped off the bus and scattered. Four of them managed to escape, but out of them, only two are currently alive. So that when I got off the bus, I expected a burst of gunfire any minute, since the two others fell by the bus right away, I stepped over the dead bodies, who had been taken out and killed prior to that. Since there was a depression there, I lay down over the bodies. This depression was some two to three metres deep, I'm not exactly sure. And I got down between those dead bodies. In the meantime, shots were heard directed at those that had escaped. And then everything got calm. The ones that had been firing came to the door. I didn't see that, as I was lying down there in that hole, but this is the picture that I created in my mind. The one that stood next to the door in front, it was probably him, said, "There are three who are alive and got out." All of this was taking place at night. I'm not sure of the exact time but it was night-time. Could have been 8.00, 9.00, 10.00, I have no idea but it was night-time. So this one man said that some were still alive, and the other one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. asked for the torch light. And then, using the flashlight, he illuminated the area, covering the dead bodies, and he saw that -- or rather, he said, "Fuck his mother, look at this guy. He's alive." Then there was a burst of gunfire and the same happened to the other man. He would illuminate the area with the flashlight and then after that, there would follow a burst of gunfire. At the same time, people that had been taken out prior to that and who had been hit by a bullet did not die immediately, and what -- one could hear moaning. And then the armed people shot at them. I remember hearing the words to the effect, "Look at these fighters. They have stone hearts." And this word "fighters" that referred to them, and I don't know what was the message, what were they trying to say, because we had not been arrested as soldiers. Then they cursed their Muslim mothers, saying, "Look at them, they have stone hearts." Then it was my turn. He took the flashlight, illuminated the area, and since I lay on my stomach, I felt the light above my head. At that moment, that person cursed again and said, "Here is another one that's alive." Excuse me. Then he took the rifle and there followed a burst of gunfire and then again with the flashlight he covered the area and then there was another burst of gunfire. So that this lasted until he ran out of ammunition. After the third burst of gunfire, a car came, and one of them said that they should use the lights on the car to illuminate the entire area because there were others that were still alive. However, since this was in a depression, the car probably could not illuminate the area so that he managed to shoot two more bursts of gunfire. After these five rounds, he ran out of ammunition. And he asked for a pistol. Somebody give it to him and then he shot two, three, four bullets around him, again used the flashlight in the area where I was. Then he took the pistol and again fired a couple of bullets more, illuminated with the flashlight again and then for the nth time cursed my mother and said, "This guy is not normal. He's still breathing.". However, the soldier, a uniformed man or somebody standing next to him, belonging to the escort that was on the bus, and that killed the people, one of them told him on a few occasions that nobody else was alive, and that all had been killed. Then he cursed the man again and they started singing their war songs. "Who is saying that Serbia is little?" And so on. They turned on the car and the bus and drove off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the hole on top of the bodies for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: About 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of anyone that was killed that night?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: My school mate, Reuf Fikic from Hambarine was there. Then there was Muhic Abdulah, called Dule. Rasid Medic. Suad Mulalic. I remember their names, although I only knew nicknames of the majority of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a person called Islam Hopovac?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was from the village of Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he one of the people that were killed that night?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Besim Hegic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. He was a bus driver. I think he used to work for AutoTransport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his approximate age?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other names that you recall, the surnames only?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: There were people with the last name Muhic, Hamulic, they were from Rizvanovici. Jamastagic [phoen], Kadiric, they were from Sredice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing anyone with a surname Kekic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I do. I can't remember the first name but I know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how old this person was?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: There were two men, cousins. One was about 17 and the other one 18 or 19. Judging by their looks, I think that's how old they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recall seeing anyone with the surname Kadic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will hear further evidence in relation to an exhumation that took place in March, 2000, later on in the case. Would that be an appropriate time for a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Ms. Sutherland. How much longer will your --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half an hour. And do you think you would be in a position to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I will. I don't have many questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll try and make an effort, try and make an effort, and I suggest that we have a short break of 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it all right with you? Is it okay with the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So a 15 minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic, when you -- when you got out of the hole where the bodies were, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: As it was night time, and I didn't know the area, I headed in some direction, unknown direction, but before I did that, I was sitting there, there was a road, a macadam road, as a matter of fact, and on the other side of the road, I saw a sign, and I went to it. I couldn't see clearly, so that I had to crawl up the post with the sign to see the direction, and it said -- I can't be quite accurate, but it said "Ravska."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just pause there, witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the agreement with the Defence and the Chamber, I may lead the witness through the next few questions until we get to the next issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have our authorisation. If there is any objection forthcoming from the Defence as you go along, I'm sure they will let us know and we will decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic, did you spend the night in the forest?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following morning, did you go to a village predominantly Croat village called Stara Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I came to that village and I came across a woman, because I had never been to that place before, so I asked her, although I assumed that it could be it, I mean Stara Rijeka, and she told me that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see only old men, women and children in that village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: First I came across a little boy in a garage. He was playing with toy cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic, just pause there for a moment. I'm wanting to ask the next following questions and I want you to answer me very briefly because I want to move on to when you left on a convoy on the 21st of -- 21st of August, 1992. So did this -- did a woman in Stara Rijeka provide you with some food?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: She did. That woman gave me food, and the next woman I came across, she told me that her husband and her two sons had been taken away. I believe her name was Kata or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this -- when was the last time you received food? Were you given any food in Miska Glava?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, none. They wouldn't even give us water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you hadn't eaten for approximately seven days?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the next three or four days, you walked around, and you were in a very bad physical condition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you met up with a woman who was going to Ljubija. What did that woman who was going to Ljubija tell you about what had happened the night before -- I'm sorry, not the night before, the night that you were at the Kipe mine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that woman was not going in the direction of Ljubija. I went there, and she was headed for the next house. She was taking some grains to have them ground, to have them milled for feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you go straight to what you consider is important for the rest of the facts that he's released statements about because I think basically, we.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic did you return to the place of the massacre at Kipe?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I did. After a few days of walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see when you returned there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I came up to that place and I saw parts -- I mean one could still see parts of footwear or jackets and there was a lot of blood. I mean this whole place was covered up, I suppose, an earth mover had come and covered it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you then spent the next few days in Stara Rijeka and then you were in the forest for approximately ten days?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I was in Stara Rijeka for a few days before I turned up again in that place where it all had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the forest for approximately ten days, you met up with three friends, Armin Petrovac, Sead Crljenkovic, and Eniz Jujic and you were shot at in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It is. One of those three had -- was wounded in the leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, when you were in the forest, did you hear about a convoy leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that convoy leaving from Tukovi and going to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right. It left from Tukovi and it was said that it would go in the direction of Travnik. That was the information that I was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point you left the forest and went to Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, approximately how many other civilians were there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but there must have been 200, 300, maybe even as many as 400 but I cannot guarantee that. Quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: The 21st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many buses and trucks were at Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that now because I dared not look around. I was too frightened. I was -- I was afraid. I don't know what. I was simply afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers there or policemen?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, not in Tukovi, but as we set off between Banja Luka and Vlasic or Skender, I'm not quite sure but I think it was that road, there was this soldier in a uniform, and he had a magnum pistol, and he had a belt with bullets in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I think he was Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I knew him -- I mean I didn't know him personally but I used to come across him in Prijedor before the war because before the war, I went to school, so that I was often there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you see him around Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In coffee shops there, or just in passing. That was before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say his name was Mrdjan or Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mrdja but whether that is his name or a nickname, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you got on to the truck at Tukovi, you proceeded towards the crossroads, Prijedor-Banja Luka road and the Kozarac-Trnopolje road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in your statement of 1995, it said that you stopped at the Trnopolje camp when in fact you stopped at the crossroads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't stop by the camp. It was the Prijedor-Kozarac road and at that place, yes, there was this crossroad where there were -- a road branched off to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the guards that were escorting the convoy asked you for money and valuables?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you stopped the second time, I think this is the time where you say you recognised the person you referred to as Mrdja, what happened at that place when you stopped? If you could explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: When we stopped there, since there was a bloke in the bus who was ordered by those soldiers to collect money or valuables, because they would simply come and say, "We want, for instance, 5.000 marks." Or, say 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you stopped at the place near Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, there was talk -- or rather it was said that women and children should move. I was in a trailer truck. And it was said that women and children should move over to -- closer to the driver. And that men should stay in the rear part of the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, were men asked to get off the trucks and the buses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No. It was said that ten guys, I mean ten men, should get ready to get off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, not from our truck fortunately, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see men getting off other trucks and buses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the convoy then move off towards Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: You mean off the truck?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, where did you get off the truck?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: On Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you walk to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of the people on the convoy that left Tukovi and the Trnopolje camp, the trucks that met at the crossroads from the Trnopolje camp, did you all arrive in Travnik that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't. Unfortunately. Because when we left Tukovi, there were lots of families there, and when we arrived in Travnik, those people who were taken out that day, they were with those, with those -- with families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people did not make it to Travnik that day?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: A list was made, one of those days, I think about 150 or something men, males.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides Mrdja, did you recognise anybody else that was escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No, not one of the escorts but I remember a truck driver, a man who used to drive a Prijedor bus, a city bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No. I don't. I only know he was a bus driver, rather the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father died on the 21st of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was he killed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: In the village of Biscani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the date is correct, the date suggested to you, the 21st of July, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I am not sure about the date, but it was a day when Biscani was cleansed and I think it was the 22nd. I'm sorry about this, but it was that day when the village was cleansed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your brother told you about the killing of your father when you met up with him later?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he eye witnessed this killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you the circumstances of your father's death in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. An armed soldier asked who was with whom, and my father said that he was with him, that he was his son, and he said, "Well, one of you has to die."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your father or your brother armed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other close relatives did you lose in the conflict which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occurred in the Prijedor municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, what we call they are cousins, that is my uncles, my brother -- my father's brother, three sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are their names? You mentioned Irfan Nasic earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Emsud Nasic, Ibrahim Nasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Trbojevic? Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Nasic, I do not have many questions and I'm really sorry to have to remind you of all these events but I'll have to ask you to try and explain certain things to us. You told us that you did your military service with the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your combat assignment after that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Combat assignment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: All I remember is that when I was leaving the army, the battalion or brigade commander said, in case of anything, I think you will be called up to -- now, what's it called? To back to this brigade, with which I'd done my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't join the reserves?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: No. I suppose that was how it was before, for those who served in Kosovo because -- and I served in Kosovo, then for a few years after that, you'd be exempt from any reserve service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the TO when these things started in 1992.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those were just village patrols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nasic and Mr. Trbojevic, please allow a short interval between answer -- question and answer and vice versa, so that we help the interpreters in their difficult job a little bit more than we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Territorial Defence unit which according to some information we have had an office in the neighbourhood community centre, didn't it? And it was supposed to have some weapons, some Territorial Defence weapons that had been distributed earlier, isn't it? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: That's true. Some weapons there were, perhaps a couple of rifles, old ones, some drum rifles, as they used to call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the chief activities were those village patrols, simply to see who is coming, who is going, and who is passing through, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any cooperation between the relevant Territorial Defence units in adjacent areas and between them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when the attack on Hambarine started, that plan was to defend Hambarine, at least as long as people would need to withdraw into the woods?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it some agreement that you reached in the neighbourhood community or in some place where this group of people decided that they would take a position and try to hold on to it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, it was more or less villagers there, local people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you -- one would know should be somebody who would be in command, who would say when to open fire, when to stop the fire?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't really privy to this kind of thing. I think that it -- Agan Sikiric was the TO commander, but I didn't really -- but I wasn't really privy to any detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw the Serbs advancing with a mechanised units that they were very strong and that they therefore any attempt to resist would be in vain and that you waited for people to pull out and then you pulled out from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember saying that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will remind you on page 2 of your statement, the one of 1995, you say, "We tried to get people out of the village and defend the village but then the Serbs came with artillery and infantry. We saw that we absolutely stood no fighting chance and therefore we withdrew to the forest?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I mentioned today but this had to do with the artillery firing from the rear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you retreated from Hambarine before the Serb infantry reached the village? Started moving from house to house?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that in this attack on Hambarine, except as a result of artillery attacks, there were no other casualties which would be due to the entry of the troops in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not see anyone injured at the time but I did hear about woundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, that first moment after you left, I suppose you turned back to see what the village looked like. Were there many houses set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Not straight away, but as the time went by, more and more houses were set on fire and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say as the time went by, do you mean the day, hours after it, or some days later?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain this to us? You said that a group of people went to the water and were killed. You mentioned this on page 3 of your 1995 statement. You said, "The following morning four of our men were killed when they went for water. Some of our men had rifles and machine-guns, and they went to where the man had been shot in order to defend the rest of us and allow us to get away." That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to that paragraph, Mr. Nasic made a correction to that statement. He didn't say rifles and machine-guns, he said only rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've heard the question. You've also heard the remark by Ms. Sutherland. What's your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the lady from the Prosecution said, those were not machine-guns, those were personal weapons, which we used in order to try and defend ourselves. Or rather the people who were armed tried to defend us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that, when you describe that the soldiers appeared and that about 500 people scattered away and then grouped in people of 50 or 150 and then there was a group of 114, you always said that nobody else in the group had any weapons any more. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he testified today that some people in the group did have some weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I would rather let him answer the question rather than intervene or interrupt in this way. Yes. Did you understand Mr. Trbojevic's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And what's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Mrs. Sutherland said, I've already said that those were just pistols. When one says weaponry, on weapons, that can refer to rifles, machine-guns, all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that answer, Mr. Trbojevic? Shall we move to something else or do you want to put further questions on the same topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We can go on and Your Honours will evaluate the evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that, you described the situation where you entered the Serb village, were encircled and detained. I'm now reading from your statement where you say that, "One man tried to escape but one of the soldiers killed him with an automatic rifle." And then you go on to say, "We had to bury him in the field." That's on page three of your statement, 1995 statement. In your 1994 statement, using the only possible logic, you say, "We went on." And this is in reference to the same situation. "So we went on and passed two Muslim villages entered by mistake the Serbian village." This corresponds to the other statement. And then you go on to say, "There we were encircled by the Chetniks" and this is as in the last statement. Then you go on to say, "Muhamed, called Duca, started fleeing from the column and one Chetnik firing from the Pap rifle hit him directly in the head and he dropped dead." Is the same event described in these two statements?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I think there was a misunderstanding there. It is the same event, the same man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on one occasion, you used the automatic rifle, on the second time, you say the PAP rifle?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Today, in my testimony, I pointed out that that was the PAP rifle. I made a lot of corrections because when I gave that statement, I did not agree with some things, because the interpreter had probably made a mistake. Just like in that case, instead of the PAP rifle, they put in the automatic rifle. However, it was the PAP rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This 1994 statement, where it says centre of security services in Banja Luka, was probably given in Travnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 1994 statement, on page 2, where I just read an excerpt from, you said that on the 26th of July, after spending two nights and one day in the forest and so on, a courier came and told us to gather and head towards Bihac. That's what you said. Can you tell us whose courier was it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. That wasn't a courier. We had a plan to set out towards the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says "courier" here and there was no interpreting involved when giving the statement. Could you have possibly said "courier" or there was no courier at all?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: As we were in groups, we had no means of communication, and probably because of that, in order for the groups to communicate between themselves, that is probably why I said a courier, because that was a means of communication between the groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same page, you said that "upon being taken to Miska Glava, that the following day, people were called out one by one and interrogated and beaten, and then on the second day, ten young men from Rizvanovici were taken out and killed there." That's what you said. In your 1995 statement, when describing that event, on page 3 of that statement, you said that "the military police came and took ten men away from Rizvanovici village and that they had not been seen since." It seems that these two descriptions are not quite identical, are they?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The story involved three men, three young men. I don't know if this is mentioned in any of these statements. I believe that one of them was from Cazin area. One was from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this group.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, when you described this in Travnik, you said that a list was used to call out a group of ten men who were immediately killed there. I am now retelling what you said, but along those lines. You said the following day, we were called out from that list, interviewed and beaten. The next day, ten young men from Rizvanovici were called out and killed right there. This is what you said, whereas in the statement that you gave the following year to the Prosecution, you said the military police came and took ten men from Rizvanovici village and they were not seen afterwards. In the first statement, there is no mention of the military police. You said that they were killed immediately, whereas the event is described in different terms in the other statement.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, but there must have been a mistake there. Three young men were taken away. As to for these men from Rizvanovici, they were taken out too and they never reappeared later on, and I assumed that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, and since you moved in that area, can you tell me what time of the day was it when the attack on Carakovo started?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was just a search in Carakovo during which a lot of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it at night, in the evening hours, early morning hours, at mid-day? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Those were early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, as your convoy entered Tukovi, there were no formalities involved, were there, no formal procedure, no documents were shown; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You simply entered and got on to a truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN NASIC
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Janu would like to ask some questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
